So, the floor rules. I'm Sonali, the floor rep on the third floor. There were twelve of us and everyone was bothered about something: late music, the shared kettle, guests.
I could have written a list and stuck it on the door, but it would have been ignored by the next day. So I called a meeting on Sunday, brought biscuits and said, we all live here, so let's decide together. Irfan, from the end room, said late music was the worst thing. Others argued about the kettle. It took two hours.
In the end we agreed on quiet after eleven, a kettle rota and guests signed in. Nobody loved every rule, but nobody could say it was forced on them. Two months later, the sheet is still up, and people actually follow it.

qa.q: How many people lived on Sonali's floor?
Why did Sonali choose a meeting over writing a list?
qa.a: Sonali knew a list would be ignored by the next day and wanted the floor to feel it was their own decision.

qa.q: What could the floor do if the rules started to slip?
qa.a: They could hold another short meeting and change the rota together, since rules made together are easier to keep than ones from one person.

qa.q: How did Irfan see the problems on the floor?
qa.a: Irfan from the end room said late music was the worst thing, so probably wanted the meeting to deal with noise most of all.

grounding: A hostel floor deciding on shared rules holds a meeting, since a plan made by one person would not be followed by the rest.

passage: I'm Pranav, and I live on the third floor of the hostel. Our floor had fights about everything: music at night, the fridge, bathroom cleaning. Gautam, our floor rep, could have just written rules and pinned them up. Instead, one evening, he knocked on all twelve doors and said, "Common room, eight o'clock, everyone." I asked him later why he didn't just decide. He said, "If I make the rules alone, nobody will follow them. Everyone uses the floor, so everyone has to agree." At the meeting people argued, laughed and voted. Quiet hours after eleven. Fridge cleaned Sundays. A cleaning rota by room. It took ninety minutes. Six weeks later, the rules on the notice board are still being followed.

qa.q: How many doors did Gautam knock on?
What was Gautam thinking when he called a meeting instead of deciding alone?
qa.a: He felt sure rules made alone wouldn't be followed, and hoped a shared decision would stick.

qa.q: Why did a group meeting suit this problem?
qa.a: Everyone shares the floor, so rules everyone helped make are more likely to be accepted and followed.

qa.q: How might the other residents see the meeting?
qa.a: They likely felt heard and more willing to follow rules they had voted on.

grounding: A hostel floor deciding on shared rules holds a meeting, since rules made by one person would not be accepted by the rest.

Monday: On the mixed second floor of the student residence, Devika was the new floor rep. The kitchen was a mess, and someone had written angry notes on the fridge. She thought about writing the rules herself. "But fourteen people use this kitchen. If I decide alone, half of them will ignore it."

Wednesday: She called a floor meeting in the kitchen. Ojas grumbled, "Just tell us the rules." "No," Devika said. "You'll follow them better if you make them." People suggested ideas; some argued. They voted: dishes washed the same night, a shelf per room, a weekly cleaning turn.

Two weeks later: The angry notes were gone. Ojas had even drawn a cleaning chart for the fridge door.

qa.q: How many people use the kitchen?
How did Ojas feel about the meeting at first?
qa.a: Ojas was impatient and grumpy, wanting to just be told the rules.

qa.q: Why did Devika choose a group meeting rather than deciding alone?
qa.a: Because many people share the kitchen, and rules they make together are more likely to be accepted and followed.

qa.q: How might the other residents see the kitchen two weeks later?
qa.a: They likely feel relieved and calmer, with the angry notes gone and rules they voted on being followed.

grounding: A residence floor deciding on shared rules holds a meeting, since rules made by one person would not be accepted or followed.
